practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the linear design strategy?
A) A cyclic process that repeats until the product meets the specification
B) A step-by-step sequence that does not loop back to earlier stages
C) A process that places the user at the centre of every design decision
D) An approach that considers the environmental impact of the whole product lifecycle
practice_questions.marks: B) A step-by-step sequence that does not loop back to earlier stages [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two design strategies that would be suitable when designing a product intended to be used by people of all ages and abilities.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: inclusive design / user-centred design (accept either or both). Accept ergonomic design with a valid brief justification. Do not accept vague answers such as 'a good strategy' with no named strategy. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using an iterative design strategy rather than a linear design strategy when developing a new type of medical monitoring device.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant advantage (e.g. 'the design can be improved through repeated cycles'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'problems discovered during testing can be fed back into the design, so errors are corrected before manufacture'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation applied to the medical device context (e.g. 'because a medical device must be highly reliable and its requirements may not be fully known at the start, iterative cycles of testing and refinement allow the team to discover and fix faults progressively, reducing the risk of producing a device that fails in clinical use'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the ergonomic design strategy. Give one example of a product where this strategy would be particularly appropriate and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): ergonomic design optimises the fit between a product and the human body, using anthropometric data about body dimensions to ensure comfort, safety and efficient use (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement mentioning the human body or anthropometrics).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, an office chair — the seat height, back support angle and armrest position must match a wide range of user body dimensions so that workers can sit safely for extended periods without developing musculoskeletal strain (2 marks for a specific, well-explained example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
An engineering company is designing a new public water fountain intended for installation in a city park. The fountain will be used by adults, children, wheelchair users and people with visual impairments.

Discuss which design strategy or strategies would be most appropriate for this project.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two appropriate strategies (e.g. inclusive design to serve diverse users including wheelchair users and visually impaired people; user-centred design to involve users in testing; ergonomic design to ensure correct operating heights and reach). Each strategy is explained with reasons linked to the scenario, with comparison of their relative suitability. Both the strengths of the recommended approach and the challenges or limitations are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant strategies identified and explained with some reference to the fountain scenario, but without full comparison or discussion of limitations.
Developing (2 marks): One relevant strategy identified and briefly explained, or two strategies named without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development or no named strategy. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is deciding whether to use a linear or iterative design strategy to develop a completely new type of electric bicycle that incorporates several untested technologies.

Evaluate which design strategy would be more appropriate for this project. Use your knowledge of both strategies to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that clearly explains the key features of both linear and iterative design, argues persuasively for iterative design given the novelty and technical uncertainty of the product, and addresses the counter-argument (linear design is cheaper and faster if requirements are well-defined — but they are not here). The answer reaches a clear, reasoned judgement with evidence from the scenario (untested technologies, need for repeated testing and refinement). Quality of written communication is high and terminology is precise.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both strategies described accurately, at least two reasons given for preferring iterative design applied to the scenario, and an attempt at a judgement, but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): One or both strategies described, some relevant reasoning, but largely one-sided or without a clear evaluative judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of one strategy with little or no comparison or application to the electric bicycle scenario. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the purpose of a design brief?
A) A document listing the materials to be used during manufacture
B) A document issued by the client outlining the problem, the user and any constraints
C) A checklist used to evaluate a finished product against ACCESS FM criteria
D) A record of all changes made during the iterative cycle
practice_questions.marks: B) A document issued by the client outlining the problem, the user and any constraints [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two activities that are carried out during the Design stage of the iterative design process.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: analysis of the design brief / researching product requirements (primary or secondary) / production of an engineering design specification / generation of design ideas by sketching and modelling. Accept any two clearly distinct activities. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using primary research over secondary research when gathering information for a new product.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. 'primary research is specific to the product'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'because it collects first-hand data directly from the intended users, so the information reflects their actual needs rather than a generalised or outdated source'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation with an applied example (e.g. 'for example, interviewing potential users of a new ergonomic tool reveals exactly how and where they hold it, which anthropometric data tables alone could not provide'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the term 'modelling' in the iterative design process. Give one example of a reason why a designer would make a model before manufacturing a prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): modelling involves creating a representation of the design — either virtual (using CAD software) or physical (using cheap materials such as card or foam) — to test specific aspects of the design without the full cost of manufacture (2 marks for a clear, developed description covering both types; 1 mark for a basic statement about making a model).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a designer might create a physical card model of a handheld device to test whether the proportions feel comfortable in the user's hand before committing to expensive tooling (2 marks for a specific, well-explained reason; 1 mark for a vague reason). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is using the iterative design process to develop a new type of adjustable bicycle helmet. They have completed one cycle of design, make and evaluate, and the prototype does not fully meet the design specification.

Discuss what the team should do next and why the iterative process is beneficial in this situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion explaining that the team should return to the design stage, analyse the evaluation feedback, modify the design ideas, produce a revised model and then a new prototype, and compare against the specification again. The discussion explains why iteration is beneficial (problems are caught and corrected progressively, reducing the risk of a flawed final product) and also acknowledges a limitation (additional cycles cost time and money, so there must be a point where the team commits to a final design). Both aspects are developed with reference to the helmet scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): The next steps are correctly identified and at least one benefit of iteration is explained with reference to the scenario, but the discussion may lack balance or depth.
Developing (2 marks): The idea of going back to the design stage is mentioned but not explained, or the benefit of iteration is stated but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A company designing a new children's educational toy has used both primary and secondary research during the Design stage of the iterative process.

Evaluate the extent to which a combination of primary and secondary research produces more useful information for writing a design specification than using only one type of research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that clearly explains what each research type provides (primary: first-hand, product-specific user data from interviews, focus groups, anthropometrics; secondary: existing knowledge including ACCESS FM analysis of competing toys and market research), argues persuasively that combining both produces richer specification criteria (primary gives specific user insights; secondary gives broader context and saves time), and addresses the counter-argument (primary research alone might suffice if the user group is well-represented and resources are available; secondary alone might be adequate for a product in a well-documented market). A clear judgement is reached, supported by the educational toy context. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both research types are described accurately, reasons for using both are given with some application to the toy scenario, and an attempt at a judgement is made, but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Both research types are mentioned but mainly described rather than evaluated, or the argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of one or both research types with little or no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a quantitative specification criterion?
A) The product must have a professional appearance
B) Users must find the product easy to hold
C) The product must weigh no more than 350 g
D) The product must look modern and stylish
practice_questions.marks: C) The product must weigh no more than 350 g [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a 'need' and a 'want' in a design specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining a need (a need is an essential requirement without which the product cannot fulfil its purpose or may be unsafe). 1 mark for defining a want (a want is a desirable but optional feature that would improve the product but is not essential to its core function). Accept equivalent wording. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a design specification should include both quantitative and qualitative criteria.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that both types are needed (e.g. 'neither type alone is sufficient'). 2 marks for explaining what each type adds (e.g. 'quantitative criteria are measurable and allow the designer to objectively test whether the prototype passes or fails; qualitative criteria capture aspects such as aesthetics and user satisfaction that cannot be reduced to a number'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation that links both types to the design process (e.g. 'together they give the design team complete targets: quantitative criteria ensure functional performance, while qualitative criteria ensure the product meets user expectations that numbers alone cannot describe — both are needed to evaluate the design fairly'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is writing a specification for a new portable outdoor camping stove. Describe two specification criteria the designer should include, using the ACCESS FM framework. For each criterion, state which ACCESS FM heading it falls under.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per criterion (1 mark for a clearly stated criterion; 1 mark for correctly identifying the ACCESS FM heading and briefly explaining why it is relevant to this product). Example acceptable answers: Safety — the stove must meet BS EN 521 standards for portable appliances using liquefied petroleum gas, to ensure it does not create a fire or explosion risk in outdoor use (2 marks). Size — the stove must fold to no larger than 150 mm × 100 mm × 40 mm when packed, so that it fits inside a standard day-pack (2 marks). Accept any two well-reasoned criteria with correct ACCESS FM headings. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is writing the specification for a new ergonomic office chair aimed at people who spend more than six hours per day at a desk. The client has stated that the chair must be both functional and visually appealing.

Discuss why it is important for the specification to include both needs and wants, and both quantitative and qualitative criteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that explains the distinction between needs and wants with examples applied to the chair (e.g. adjustable lumbar support = need; fabric colour choice = want) and between quantitative and qualitative criteria (e.g. seat height adjustable 400–520 mm = quantitative; fabric must feel premium to professional users = qualitative). The discussion explains how both pairs of concepts work together to produce a complete, testable specification, and acknowledges potential tensions (e.g. wants may have to be sacrificed if the cost budget is tight; qualitative criteria are harder to test objectively). Both benefits and limitations are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least one example each of a need and a want, and at least one each of a quantitative and qualitative criterion, with some explanation of why both are included — but may lack balance or depth.
Developing (2 marks): The terms are used but not clearly explained or applied to the chair scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A company is designing a new range of children's bicycle helmets for ages 5–10. The design team has written an initial specification using the ACCESS FM framework, but the project manager says the criteria are too vague to be useful for evaluating prototypes.

Evaluate the importance of writing precise, measurable specification criteria and consider whether there are any situations where qualitative criteria are unavoidable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that precise, measurable (quantitative) criteria are essential because they allow objective pass/fail testing of prototypes against the specification, cite specific examples relevant to the helmet (e.g. impact absorption standard in joules, mass limit in grams, retention system release force in Newtons), and that vague criteria lead to subjective and inconsistent evaluation. The response then addresses the counter-argument: some criteria genuinely cannot be quantified — the appearance of a children's helmet must appeal to children and parents, and this can only be assessed through user testing and focus groups, making qualitative criteria unavoidable in any real specification. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about how to handle the balance, supported by the helmet scenario. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): The importance of quantitative criteria is clearly argued with at least two examples, qualitative criteria are acknowledged as necessary for some aspects, and an attempt at a judgement is made — but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Both types of criteria are discussed but mainly described rather than evaluated, or the argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about specifications with little or no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a wasting manufacturing process?
A) Injection moulding
B) Bending sheet metal
C) CNC milling
D) Powder coating
practice_questions.marks: C) CNC milling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which the scale of manufacture influences engineering design.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: one-off production allows complex, bespoke geometry but has very high unit cost / batch production requires designs suitable for flexible tooling or standard material forms / mass production requires design for automated assembly (e.g. draft angles for moulding, uniform wall thickness) / mass production justifies high capital investment in dedicated tooling / low-volume designs should use low-tooling processes to avoid unrecoverable capital costs. Accept any two clearly distinct design implications. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between labour costs and capital costs in manufacturing, and give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly distinguishing the two (labour = cost of human work; capital = cost of machinery and tooling). 2 marks for one example of each (e.g. labour: wages paid to assembly-line workers fitting components by hand; capital: the cost of purchasing a new injection-mould tool). 3 marks for a developed explanation that connects both to a design decision (e.g. 'to reduce labour costs, the designer simplifies the assembly sequence so fewer workers are needed; to justify capital costs, the product must be produced in high volumes, which influences whether the designer specifies injection moulding or a lower-tooling process such as laser cutting'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A company plans to manufacture a new plastic housing for an industrial sensor in batches of 200 units twice per year. Describe two manufacturing considerations the designer should take into account when designing the housing.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per consideration (1 mark for identifying a relevant consideration; 1 mark for explaining how it affects the design of the housing at this batch scale). Example acceptable answers: Scale of manufacture — at a batch of 200, injection moulding is unlikely to recover the mould-tool capital cost; the designer should specify a wasting process such as CNC machining from standard nylon block, or vacuum forming from sheet, both of which have lower tooling costs appropriate for this volume (2 marks). Material availability and form — the designer should specify the housing in a standard sheet or block size to minimise material waste and ensure reliable supply, avoiding a bespoke cross-section that would require expensive extrusion tooling (2 marks). Accept any two well-reasoned considerations applied to the batch scenario. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
An engineering company is redesigning a metal bracket that is currently made by a wasting process (CNC milling from solid bar). The company wants to reduce production costs now that demand has increased to 50,000 units per year.

Discuss what manufacturing considerations the design team should take into account when redesigning the bracket for higher-volume production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant considerations applied to the scenario — for example: switching to a forming process (stamping or press forming) at this volume justifies the capital cost of a press tool and dramatically reduces labour and material waste compared to machining; material form should be changed to standard sheet or coil stock rather than solid bar; labour costs can be further reduced by designing the bracket for automated press-feed rather than manual loading. The discussion acknowledges trade-offs: the redesigned bracket may have slightly different geometry constraints (minimum bend radius, material springback) that the designer must accommodate. Both benefits and limitations are addressed with reference to the 50,000-unit scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant considerations identified and explained with some reference to the volume change, but without full comparison or discussion of constraints.
Developing (2 marks): One relevant consideration identified, or two mentioned without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A start-up company has designed a new ergonomic hand tool for professional tradespeople. The first production run will be 500 units, but if the product succeeds, volumes could rise to 100,000 units per year within three years.

Evaluate the extent to which manufacturing considerations should influence the initial design of the hand tool, given the uncertainty about future production volumes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that manufacturing considerations are central even for the initial 500-unit run — material form, process type and production cost must all be considered to keep unit costs viable — but that the uncertainty about future volumes creates a genuine design tension: designing purely for 500 units (e.g. CNC machined aluminium alloy) may mean the design must be fundamentally revised for mass production (e.g. redesigned for die casting), adding cost and delay. The response argues that a forward-looking design strategy — using processes that scale (e.g. investment casting with low-volume tooling that can be upgraded) and designing the geometry to be compatible with both batch and high-volume processes — is the most appropriate approach, but acknowledges that this adds complexity and cost to the initial design stage. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about how much manufacturing consideration is appropriate at the early stage. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): Manufacturing considerations for both production levels are addressed, at least two specific factors are linked to the hand-tool scenario, and an attempt at a judgement about the tension is made — but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Manufacturing considerations are discussed but mainly descriptively, or the argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about manufacturing with little or no evaluation of the uncertainty. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes 'technology push'?
A) Consumer demand for a product with longer battery life drives manufacturers to improve battery design
B) A new carbon-fibre composite material becomes available and enables the design of lighter, stronger bicycle frames
C) Legislation requires manufacturers to remove a hazardous material from their products
D) A company deliberately limits a product's lifespan to encourage repeat purchases
practice_questions.marks: B) A new carbon-fibre composite material becomes available and enables the design of lighter, stronger bicycle frames [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the 6Rs of sustainable design.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Rethink / Reuse / Recycle / Repair / Reduce / Refuse. Accept any two correctly named Rs. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'planned obsolescence' and give one reason why it conflicts with sustainable design principles.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining planned obsolescence (e.g. 'designing a product with a deliberately limited lifespan to encourage the consumer to replace it'). 2 marks for identifying a conflict with sustainability (e.g. 'this conflicts with the Repair principle of the 6Rs, because a product designed to be difficult to repair generates waste that would otherwise be avoided'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation linking planned obsolescence to a specific 6R and explaining the environmental consequence (e.g. 'it also conflicts with Reduce because artificially short product lifespans increase the total number of products manufactured, consuming more raw materials and energy than necessary — the opposite of what sustainable design aims to achieve'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the UKCA mark. Give one example of how compliance with the UKCA mark influences a design decision.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the UKCA (United Kingdom Conformity Assessed) mark may be used for certain regulated products placed on the Great Britain market. The applicable marking depends on the product rules, and CE marking continues to be recognised for many products (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that it is a UK conformity mark).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a designer specifying insulation for an electrical product must meet the relevant product-safety requirements before placing it on the market — this constrains material choice even if another material is cheaper (2 marks for a specific, well-explained example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer of domestic power tools is reviewing its product range in response to growing consumer demand for sustainable products and new legislation on product repairability.

Discuss how sustainable design principles and legislation together influence the design of the manufacturer's next power drill.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that addresses at least two sustainable design principles (e.g. Repair — design the drill so that brushes, batteries and switches can be user-replaced; Reduce — lightweight housing through material optimisation; Refuse — avoid non-recyclable composite materials for the housing) and connects them to legislation (for example, where product-specific rules require spare parts or repair information). The discussion explains how both forces pull in the same direction for this product but may also create tensions (e.g. designing for repairability may increase initial manufacturing cost or reduce robustness). Both benefits and challenges are addressed with reference to the drill scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant sustainable design points and a reference to legislation, with some explanation applied to the power drill, but without full discussion of tensions or limitations.
Developing (2 marks): One relevant point about sustainability or legislation, briefly explained.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A global electronics company is under increasing commercial pressure to release new smartphone models every twelve months, using planned obsolescence to drive sales. At the same time, the company has publicly committed to designing for the circular economy.

Evaluate the extent to which planned obsolescence and circular economy design can coexist in the same product development strategy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that clearly explains planned obsolescence (deliberate limitation of product lifespan to drive repeat sales — commercial rationale is strong in a competitive market) and the circular economy (designing to keep products and materials in productive use as long as possible — keeping higher-value loops like repair and remanufacturing ahead of recycling). The response argues that the two approaches are fundamentally in conflict: planned obsolescence shortens product life deliberately, while the circular economy extends it deliberately. However, it then addresses the nuance: a company can commit to circular material recovery (recycling and modular design for component reuse) while still releasing annual models — the conflict is most severe when obsolescence prevents repair or component recovery. The response reaches a clear, reasoned judgement that the two strategies cannot fully coexist at the product level without compromise, but that partial circular design (modular batteries, repairability, take-back schemes) can reduce the environmental cost of an inevitably short product cycle. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both concepts are described accurately, the fundamental tension is identified and discussed with some application to the smartphone scenario, and an attempt at a judgement is made — but the nuance or counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Both concepts are mentioned but the evaluation is largely one-sided or descriptive, without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of one or both concepts with little or no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which drawing type shows a 3D object with horizontal edges drawn at 30° to the base line?
A) Oblique
B) Freehand sketch
C) Isometric
D) Third-angle orthographic
practice_questions.marks: C) Isometric [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of engineering drawing that are used to show the logic or sequence of a system rather than its physical shape.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: block diagram / flowchart / circuit diagram / wiring diagram. Accept any two that are genuinely distinct answers from this group. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using freehand sketching during the design process.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): freehand sketching is fast / no instruments needed / allows rapid generation of ideas. Disadvantage (1 mark): lacks precision / cannot convey exact dimensions / not suitable for manufacturing. Development (1 mark): extending either point with a reason — for example, because no setting-up time is needed, a designer can explore many concepts quickly; however, without exact dimensions the sketch cannot be issued to a manufacturer as a working drawing. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of an exploded view drawing. Give one example of where it would typically be used.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): an exploded view shows all the individual components of a product separated along a common axis, with lines indicating how the parts align and fit together (2 marks for a clear developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it shows the parts apart'). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, an exploded view is used in a flat-pack furniture instruction manual to show the customer which components are present and the correct assembly sequence (2 marks for a specific applied example; 1 mark for a vague example such as 'in instructions'). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is developing an electronic alarm system. The team needs to communicate the system's circuit connections to the electronics manufacturer and also show the proposed sequence of operations to the client.

Discuss which types of engineering drawing would be most appropriate for each purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that identifies and justifies an appropriate drawing for each purpose, with reasoning applied to the scenario. For circuit connections: a circuit diagram using standard electronic symbols (BS 3939 / IEC 60617) is most appropriate because it shows exactly how each component is connected electrically, which the manufacturer needs for construction and fault-finding. For the sequence of operations: a flowchart is most appropriate because it shows the logic and decision points of the alarm's operation using standardised symbols, which the client can understand without needing electrical expertise. Both choices are developed with reasons and linked to the scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both drawing types correctly identified with some justification but limited development or scenario application.
Developing (2 marks): One drawing type correctly identified with a reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant drawing type named without justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A design engineer is choosing between isometric and third-angle orthographic projection to communicate a new mechanical component to a manufacturer.

Evaluate the extent to which isometric drawing is a suitable choice for communicating a component to a manufacturer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies the strengths of isometric drawing (realistic 3D appearance, good for visualising overall shape, easy for non-specialists to understand) and then challenges these with clear reasons why isometric is not suitable for direct manufacture (lines are drawn to true length but dimensions are not annotated in a standard manufacturing format, hidden detail cannot be shown, tolerances and surface finish cannot be specified). The response reaches a substantiated judgement — for example, that isometric is suitable for presenting the concept to a client but third-angle orthographic projection must be used for manufacture because it provides front, plan and end views with full dimensioning, tolerances and line-type conventions that a manufacturer requires.
Secure (5–6 marks): The strengths and limitations are identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points are largely one-sided (either only advantages or only disadvantages) with limited judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about isometric drawing with no evaluation or judgement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
In a UK third-angle orthographic drawing, where is the plan view positioned relative to the front view?
A) Below the front view
B) To the left of the front view
C) Above the front view
D) To the right of the front view
practice_questions.marks: C) Above the front view [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two items of information that must be included in the title block of an engineering drawing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: drawing title / drawing number / designer's name / date / scale / sheet size / material / finish / projection symbol / revision history. Accept any two clearly different items. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a hidden detail line and an outline on an engineering drawing.
practice_questions.marks: Outline (1 mark): a continuous thick line showing visible edges of the object. Hidden detail (1 mark): a thin dashed line showing edges or surfaces that are hidden behind other features in that view. Development (1 mark): for example, if a blind hole is drilled into a block, the bottom of the hole cannot be seen in the front view, so it is shown as a thin dashed line to indicate its presence without it being visible. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a tolerance on an engineering drawing. Give one example of why tolerances are important in manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a tolerance is the permissible range of variation in a manufactured dimension, stated as an upper and lower limit; for example ⌀25 +0.02/−0.01 mm means the diameter must be between 24.99 mm and 25.02 mm (2 marks for a developed description including both upper and lower limits; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it shows how much a dimension can vary'). Example (up to 2 marks): tolerances ensure that components are interchangeable — in mass production, if every shaft is made within its tolerance, it will fit any matching bearing without selective assembly, reducing production costs and assembly time (2 marks for a specific example; 1 mark for a vague point about accuracy). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is producing a working drawing of a machined shaft that includes a threaded section, a knurled grip and a chamfered end. The shaft must fit a matching bearing with an interference fit.

Discuss the drawing conventions and information that the student must include to communicate this component fully to a manufacturer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced response that addresses at least three of the following with explanation: third-angle orthographic projection with the correct projection symbol in the title block; correct line types (outlines, hidden detail, centre lines, dimension lines, projection lines); dimensioning of the thread using the standard thread convention (thick and thin lines, root and crest); the knurl shown with cross-hatched pattern; the chamfer shown with an angled line and dimensioned angle or linear value; a tolerance on the bearing diameter to specify the interference fit. Both the choice of convention and the reason for its importance are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two conventions identified with some explanation but limited development or missing the tolerance point.
Developing (2 marks): One or two conventions identified with minimal explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturing company uses working drawings conforming to BS 8888 to produce components that are assembled at different factories across the UK.

Evaluate the importance of using standardised drawing conventions when communicating engineering designs for manufacture.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying the strong arguments for standardisation — unambiguous communication meaning any engineer can interpret the drawing correctly; interchangeability of parts because tolerances are understood consistently; legal traceability through the title block; reduced risk of manufacturing errors and costly rework — then genuinely challenging these with counterpoints, such as the initial cost and time of training all engineers to the standard, the cost of drawing software that enforces BS 8888, and the fact that for one-off prototype work informal sketches may be faster and perfectly adequate. A clear judgement is reached — for example, that standardisation is essential for production components where accuracy and interchangeability matter, but proportionality is needed and one-off prototyping can use less formal approaches.
Secure (5–6 marks): Strengths and limitations identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Largely one-sided, focusing only on advantages with limited or no counterargument.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about standardisation with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a limitation of CAD compared to manual drawing?
A) CAD produces less accurate dimensions
B) CAD cannot produce 3D models
C) CAD requires expensive software and significant training time
D) CAD drawings cannot be shared digitally
practice_questions.marks: C) CAD requires expensive software and significant training time [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using CAD software compared to manual drawing techniques.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: greater dimensional accuracy / faster editing and revision / instant digital sharing / automatic enforcement of drawing standards / automatic generation of 2D views from 3D model / direct link to CAM manufacturing / photorealistic rendering. Accept any two clearly different advantages. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how 3D parametric CAD software improves efficiency when making design changes.
practice_questions.marks: Point (1 mark): in parametric CAD, dimensions are driven by parameters so that changing one value automatically updates all related features. Development (1 mark): for example, if a designer increases the diameter of a shaft, all features that reference that diameter — such as the shoulder length, thread engagement and related holes — update automatically. Further development (1 mark): this eliminates the need to manually update each drawing view and reduces the risk of introducing errors or inconsistencies between views, which would occur if a manual drawing was amended. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the 'digital thread' between CAD and manufacture. Give one example of how it reduces manufacturing errors.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): the digital thread refers to a direct link between a 3D CAD model and manufacturing — for example, a CAD model is sent to CAM software, which generates CNC machine toolpaths from the digital geometry without manually re-entering dimensions (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'CAD links to manufacturing'). Example (up to 2 marks): dimensions transferred from the CAD model do not need to be manually typed into a CNC program, reducing the risk of a programmer misreading a drawing (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A product design student is developing a new mechanical toy and needs to communicate the design to both a manufacturing partner and a retail client. The manufacturing partner will machine components on CNC equipment; the retail client has no technical drawing knowledge.

Discuss which digital design communication methods would be most appropriate for each audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that selects and justifies an appropriate method for each audience with reasons applied to the scenario. For the manufacturing partner: CAD working drawings (2D orthographic views with dimensions and tolerances) exported as PDF or DXF/DWG, because the manufacturer needs exact dimensions, tolerances and line-type conventions to machine components correctly; alternatively, direct CAD/CAM file transfer for CNC programming. For the retail client: a photorealistic 3D render or animation, because the client cannot read technical drawings and needs to see what the product looks like to make commercial decisions. Both choices are developed with reasons linked to the scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both audiences addressed with correct method identified but limited development or scenario application.
Developing (2 marks): One audience addressed correctly.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant point about CAD with no audience-specific application. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small engineering start-up is deciding whether to invest in professional CAD software to replace their existing manual drawing processes. The company employs five engineers who currently produce working drawings by hand.

Evaluate the extent to which investing in CAD software is worthwhile for this company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering the strong arguments for investment — increased drawing accuracy, faster revision and iteration, instant digital sharing with clients and manufacturers, direct CAM link reducing manufacturing errors, ability to create renders for client proposals, enforced drawing standards — and then genuinely challenging these with counterpoints relevant to a small start-up: high upfront cost of software licences for five users, significant training time during which productivity will fall, high-spec hardware required, and the fact that for early concept work freehand sketching remains faster and cheaper. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached that weighs these factors — for example, that the long-term productivity gains justify the investment for a company that regularly produces working drawings for manufacture, but the break-even point must be considered relative to current workload.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments for and against identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement, but the judgement may not be fully substantiated.
Developing (3–4 marks): Largely one-sided response with limited counterargument.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about CAD with no evaluation or judgement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
What is another name for the QFD evaluation tool?
A) Decision matrix
B) Ranking matrix
C) House of Quality
D) Design specification
practice_questions.marks: C) House of Quality [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two methods of evaluating design ideas that are listed in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: production of models / qualitative comparison with the design brief and specification / ranking matrix / Quality Function Deployment (QFD). Accept any two clearly different methods. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using a ranking matrix compared to a qualitative comparison when evaluating design ideas.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): a ranking matrix provides numerical scores for each design concept against weighted criteria, allowing structured comparison of multiple options. Development (1 mark): unlike qualitative comparison, which relies on descriptive judgements, the ranking matrix encourages the evaluator to apply consistent scoring to every criterion. Further development (1 mark): for example, if three concepts score 84, 71 and 63 weighted points respectively, the designer has a clear basis for selecting concept one — rather than only saying it 'looks better'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a ranking matrix is constructed and used to evaluate design ideas. Include reference to weighted criteria.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): criteria from the design specification are listed in rows and each design concept is given a column; each criterion is assigned a weighting (e.g. 1–5) reflecting its importance, and each design is scored against each criterion (e.g. 1–5); the score is multiplied by the weighting and totals are summed for each design concept (2 marks for a clear developed description including both scoring and weighting; 1 mark for a basic statement). Application (up to 2 marks): for example, if safety has a weighting of 5 and a design scores 4 for safety, its weighted score for that criterion is 20; this means safety contributes far more to the total than a criterion weighted 1, ensuring the most important requirements drive the selection decision (2 marks for a specific applied example; 1 mark for a vague point about importance). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team has produced three concept designs for a new children's ride-on toy. They need to select the best concept to develop further before prototyping.

Discuss which evaluation method(s) would be most appropriate to help the design team select the best concept, and explain the reasons for your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that selects and justifies at least two evaluation methods with reasoning applied to the scenario. A ranking matrix is well-suited because it allows all three concepts to be scored against weighted specification criteria (such as safety, cost, aesthetics and ease of manufacture) simultaneously, providing a numerical basis for selection — important for a children's product where safety must be heavily weighted. A qualitative comparison with the brief could complement this by providing written justification for scores, particularly for subjective criteria such as aesthetic appeal. The discussion addresses both the strengths and any limitations of the chosen methods in the context of selecting between three concepts.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two evaluation methods correctly identified with some justification but limited development or scenario application.
Developing (2 marks): One method identified with a reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A product design team is using QFD (Quality Function Deployment) to evaluate a new design for a portable electric drill. The customer requirements include: lightweight, comfortable grip, powerful, long battery life and affordable.

Evaluate the extent to which QFD is a useful tool for evaluating competing design concepts at this stage of the design process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying the genuine strengths of QFD in this context — it maps all five customer requirements onto engineering characteristics (motor power, battery capacity, housing weight, grip geometry, component cost), reveals the strength of each relationship, and — critically — the roof section exposes trade-offs such as the conflict between lightweight and high power (a larger, heavier motor provides more power). This is especially valuable for a complex multi-criteria product like a drill. Then genuinely challenged with counterpoints: QFD is complex to construct correctly and time-consuming; for early concept comparison it may be more effort than a ranking matrix; the quality of the output depends on correctly identifying the engineering characteristics; and it is not specifically designed to compare discrete design concepts against each other (a ranking matrix does this better). A clear judgement is reached — for example, that QFD is most valuable for understanding relationships and trade-offs between requirements rather than for ranking specific concepts, and that a ranking matrix may be more appropriate for the specific task of selecting between competing concepts.
Secure (5–6 marks): Strengths and limitations identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Largely one-sided with limited counterargument.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of QFD with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which modelling method is most appropriate for testing whether an electronic circuit works as intended before committing to a printed circuit board?
A) Card model
B) Block model
C) Breadboard
D) Virtual 3D CAD
practice_questions.marks: C) Breadboard [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of information that can be obtained from a 3D-printed prototype model.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: dimensional accuracy / surface quality / assembly fit between parts / weight / visual appearance. Accept any two clearly different items from this list. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one limitation of using virtual 3D CAD modelling to evaluate a design idea.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): no material is consumed; changes can be made instantly without discarding a physical object. Or: digital analysis of mass, stress and assembly clearance is possible without any manufacturing. Development (1 mark): for example, if a stress analysis (FEA) reveals a weak point, the model geometry can be changed and re-analysed within minutes. Limitation (1 mark): a virtual model cannot be picked up or handled, so it cannot reveal how the product feels ergonomically in the hand, or whether it can be assembled comfortably by a user. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in producing a card model and state two types of information it provides.
practice_questions.marks: Stages (up to 2 marks): draw the net of the form on card; cut along the outlines (using a scalpel and steel rule on a cutting mat); score and fold along the fold lines; glue the tabs to assemble the 3D shape; add detail features with additional card pieces (2 marks for a clear four-stage description; 1 mark for a basic description with fewer stages). Information (up to 2 marks): a card model provides information about the proportions of the design (whether it looks the right shape) and the scale (whether it is the correct physical size in the context of its intended use) — for example, placing a card model of a new phone on a desk confirms whether it looks appropriately sized next to other objects (2 marks for two clearly stated types; 1 mark for only one). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student has manufactured a prototype of a new ergonomic hand tool. The prototype needs to be evaluated before the design is finalised for production.

Discuss the methods the student should use to evaluate the prototype against the design specification.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two evaluation methods applied to the scenario. Quantitative comparison: measuring the prototype dimensions using vernier callipers or a micrometer and comparing each measured value against the specification tolerance — this objectively confirms whether dimensional requirements are met. User testing: giving the prototype to representative users and gathering structured feedback on grip comfort, ease of use and fatigue — this tests qualitative specification criteria such as ergonomics that cannot be measured with instruments. The discussion addresses both what each method reveals and why both are needed, with reference to the hand tool context.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two methods identified with some explanation and partial scenario application.
Developing (2 marks): One method described with limited application to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is choosing between breadboarding and 3D printing to model a new electronic wearable fitness tracker at the prototype stage. The product has both an electronic control circuit and a moulded plastic housing that must fit comfortably on a wrist.

Evaluate the extent to which breadboarding alone is sufficient to model this product at the prototype stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying what breadboarding can test (the electronic circuit — component values, switching behaviour, sensor operation — quickly and cheaply, with components reusable and the circuit easily modified) and then genuinely challenging this with its limitations in the context of a wearable product: breadboarding reveals nothing about the housing form, ergonomics, wrist fit, surface quality or wearability — which are equally important specification criteria for a fitness tracker. A 3D-printed housing model would be needed to test form, fit and comfort. The response reaches a clear judgement — breadboarding is necessary and sufficient for testing the electronic function, but it is not sufficient alone because it cannot address the physical and ergonomic aspects of the product; both modelling methods are needed at this stage.
Secure (5–6 marks): Strengths and limitations of breadboarding identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Largely one-sided, focusing either only on what breadboarding can test or only on its limitations, with limited judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of breadboarding with no evaluation or judgement. [8 marks]
